clue.text: Sneaks off with winter month's electric supply

parts.note: DEC is the usual abbreviation for December, a winter month
amps, units of current, stand for the electricity supplied

explanation.surface: Someone slips away taking the December electricity with them.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to leave suddenly or secretly, which is what one who sneaks off does.

clue.text: A hundred tales of French and Scottish G.P.

parts.note: de is the French word for of
Dr Cameron is the senior Scottish family doctor in A. J. Cronin's Dr Finlay stories

explanation.surface: A hundred stories about France and a Scottish country doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: A G.P. is a general practitioner, a family doctor; 'and' links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's book is a collection of a hundred stories told over ten days.

clue.text: The sweeties of Cranford?

parts.note: in Mrs Gaskell's novel Cranford, Miss Matty keeps a little shop selling sugared sweets

explanation.surface: A question about the darlings of Mrs Gaskell's genteel village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweeties' looks like a term for the village's charming ladies, but it means sugar-coated sweets of the kind sold in the novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfits are sweets made of seeds or nuts coated in sugar, an old-fashioned confection.

clue.text: Trim canes to confound an evildoer

indicators.note: confounding means throwing into confusion, so the letters of the two words are mixed

explanation.surface: Pruning canes to baffle a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to confound' rearranges TRIM CANES.
explanation.definitionFit: A miscreant is a wrongdoer or villain.

clue.text: The music of a motor-bike

explanation.surface: The sound a motorcycle makes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' links. A motorcycle ridden without a sidecar was called a solo machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece performed by one player, and a motorcycle without a sidecar, both go by this word.

clue.text: God with a winning card takes a cure!

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of shepherds and the wild
an ace is the card that beats the others in many games

explanation.surface: A deity holding a trump card walks off with a remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go down as PAN, then ACE, then the A, whatever the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a supposed remedy for every ill, a universal cure.

clue.text: A poet's involved about wine for princes

indicators.note: about puts the jumbled letters round the wine
involved means tangled up, so the letters of A POET'S are rearranged

parts.note: tent is a deep red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: A poet gets mixed up with wine meant for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges A POET'S into POATES, and 'about' wraps it round TENT, an old name for a dark Spanish red wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Potentates are monarchs or rulers, powerful sovereigns like princes.

clue.text: Such a turn as it gave me!

definitions.text: Such a turn as it gave me!

parts.words: Such a turn as it gave me!
parts.note: the exclaimed fright describes an unpleasant shock, a turn of the kind people say gave them a bad scare

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims about the fright they just had.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasty turn is the everyday phrase for an unpleasant shock or attack of faintness.

clue.text: Hill sheep

explanation.surface: Sheep grazing on the hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cheviot Hills lie on the border between England and Scotland, and give their name to a hardy breed of sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: The range on the English-Scottish border has a hill of this name, and a hardy breed of sheep comes from there.

clue.text: Continue the performance in W.3

explanation.surface: Carrying on the show in a west London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' links. W3 is the London postcode district of Acton in west London.
explanation.definitionFit: To act on is to carry on acting; the district with postcode W3 is in west London.

clue.text: Searches everywhere for old short woollies!

explanation.surface: Someone hunts all over for a set of old woollen underclothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' links the two definitions. Combinations were one-piece woollen underwear, shortened in speech to the plural word here.
explanation.definitionFit: To comb an area is to search it thoroughly; combinations, old one-piece undergarments, were called by this short name.

clue.text: Nicotiana's fragrant yield is be-coming less apparent

explanation.surface: The tobacco plant's perfume fades as it grows fainter.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicotiana, the flowering tobacco, gives off its perfume in the evening, so its fragrant yield is a 'late scent'; 'is' links that to the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Latescent means becoming latent, slowly hiding itself from view; the tobacco flower releases its perfume late in the day.

clue.text: The Master of France

parts.note: the French word for a master or teacher, as in a head waiter's title

explanation.surface: A grand title for a leading figure of France.
explanation.definitionFit: In French, the word is the ordinary term for a master, schoolmaster or head of a dining room.

clue.text: A sleeper from Beaconsfield

explanation.surface: Someone who dozes, coming from a Buckinghamshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Beaconsfield is a town in Buckinghamshire, but here it is Disraeli, made Earl of Beaconsfield, whose last novel bears this title. In Greek myth the shepherd was cast into everlasting sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical shepherd loved by Selene sleeps forever; Disraeli, Lord Beaconsfield, wrote a novel under this name.

clue.text: Crisp, hot, A1 in brief

indicators.note: to put something in brief is to recast it in a short form, so the letters are rewritten

parts.note: the figure 1 is read as the letter I, so the grade gives A and I

explanation.surface: A summary praising something as crisp, spicy and first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 gives the letters A and I. 'in brief' recasts CRISP HOT AI, and the whole clue describes the terse, punchy, first-class style of a maxim.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphoristic writing is terse and pointed, packing a sharp truth into few words.

clue.text: Car is concealed here

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are disguised, so they appear rearranged into a place name

explanation.surface: A car is stashed out of sight at this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealed' disguises CAR IS by rearranging it. RISCA is a town in Monmouthshire, south Wales; 'here' stands for the place.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition points to a place, and Risca is a town in south Wales.

clue.text: Beaumont and Fletcher, lamented by Lamb?

explanation.surface: The Jacobean playwriting pair, mourned by the essayist Charles Lamb.
explanation.walkthrough: Beaumont and Fletcher wrote plays together, so they were partners in plays. Charles Lamb's poem The Old Familiar Faces opens by lamenting those he had as a child: 'I have had playmates, I have had companions'.
explanation.definitionFit: The two dramatists were partners in writing plays; Lamb's poem mourns childhood companions in games.

clue.text: Marathon observers?

parts.note: Byron's song The Isles of Greece says that what towers over the plain looks on Marathon

explanation.surface: Spectators watching a long-distance race.
explanation.walkthrough: The race suggests runners and crowds, but Marathon is the battle plain in Greece, and Byron wrote that the peaks look on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's lines picture the high peaks round the plain of Marathon gazing down on it.

clue.text: Condemns in so many words

explanation.surface: Someone passes judgement in a few words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge condemns a convict by passing judgement on them; a sentence is a set of words making a complete statement.

clue.text: A phrase for the socially rejected in the past?

definitions.text: A phrase for the socially rejected in the past?

parts.words: A phrase for the socially rejected in the past?
parts.note: the polite formula a servant once used at the door to turn away an unwanted caller

explanation.surface: A question about what people used to call social outcasts.
explanation.walkthrough: The socially rejected are not outcasts but callers: a household once told visitors it did not wish to see that the mistress was out, whether she was or not.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was the conventional excuse given to unwelcome visitors when people paid formal calls.

clue.text: Copper -bottomed water-sprite needs combing!

indicators.note: in a down clue the copper goes at the bottom, below the sprite

parts.note: tangle, Orkney and Shetland tangie, is a sea spirit dressed in seaweed
d is the old abbreviation for a penny, a copper coin

explanation.surface: A water-spirit with a copper bottom whose hair badly wants brushing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottomed' puts D under the sprite. D was a penny in old British money, a copper coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair in knots is matted and wants the comb, so the description fits.

clue.text: 9 in this suit, but not for a Southerner!

explanation.surface: Something worn as a suit, though a man from the South would have none of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 refers to the answer at 9 across: a union suit is a one-piece undergarment. In the American Civil War the North fought for the Union, so it was not the cause of a Confederate Southerner.
explanation.definitionFit: A union suit is a one-piece combination undergarment, and the Union was the Northern side in the American Civil War.

clue.text: Toothy as an elephant

explanation.surface: Describing an elephant as having big teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivories is slang for teeth, and an elephant's tusks are ivory.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivories is slang for teeth, so one with many is toothy; an elephant's tusks give it ivory.

clue.text: Ode for a merchant banker?

parts.note: an ode in the style of the Greek poet Pindar, whose name split up gives a fastener and an ancient Persian gold coin, small change for a banker

explanation.surface: A request for a poem fit to honour a City financier.
explanation.walkthrough: A daric is an ancient Persian gold coin; with 'pin' in front, the word for a Pindar-style ode becomes money talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A poem modelled on Pindar's odes is described by the adjective formed from the poet's name.

clue.text: Ravenous poet astride a horse gets fish in plate!

indicators.note: the poet's name sits on either side of the horse, like a rider

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe wrote The Raven
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: A hungry poet mounted on a horse gets fish served on a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ravenous' is not hungry here but points to Poe, author of The Raven. The pogge, or armed bullhead, is a small fish covered in bony plates.
explanation.definitionFit: The armed bullhead, a small sea fish, has an armour of bony plates.

clue.text: Frighten, in a jolly way

parts.note: à la, French for in the manner of, is taken here as in a way
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM

explanation.surface: Scaring someone in a light-hearted manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a ... way' renders à la, 'in the manner of', and 'jolly' is a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: To alarm someone is to frighten or startle them.

clue.text: How voters fought in a mêlée

indicators.note: a mêlée is a confused scrum, so the word voters is thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: An account of an election crowd brawling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a mêlée' jumbles VOTERS; 'How' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Strove is the past tense of strive, to struggle or contend.

clue.text: He changes colour easily

parts.note: a worker whose trade is altering the colour of cloth does it without trouble

explanation.surface: Someone who blushes or turns pale at the slightest thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a person who blushes readily; the tradesman changes the colour of fabric as a matter of routine.
explanation.definitionFit: A dyer is a tradesman who colours cloth with dyes.

clue.text: Everyone in Elmer's hold shows such bravery

indicators.note: the word for everyone sits within the surname, as the clue says

parts.note: Elmer Gantry is the evangelist hero of Sinclair Lewis's novel
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Everyone held by a man named Elmer displays great courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold' belongs with the surface; the piece is Elmer's surname, from Sinclair Lewis's 1927 novel Elmer Gantry.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallantry is courage, especially dashing courage in battle.

clue.text: On the (Trojan?) flank among the Liliaceae

indicators.note: the letters wanted lie inside the plant family's name, among its letters

explanation.surface: A botanical note on the side of the lily family, with a nod to Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' sends you inside LILIACEAE. The '(Trojan?)' teases that Ilium was Troy, but the word comes from ilium, the hip bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Iliac means relating to the ilium, the bone of the hip and flank.

clue.text: When it's prevalent, the French physician is disturbed

indicators.note: the French doctor's title is shaken up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: médecin is French for a doctor

explanation.surface: A French doctor is upset when an illness is going around.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram works on a translation: 'the French physician' is MEDECIN, and 'is disturbed' rearranges those letters. 'When it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease that is endemic is regularly found among a particular people or region, so it is prevalent there.

clue.text: Lives only to be concerned about the teams

parts.note: re means regarding or about
sides are teams in a game

explanation.surface: Someone lives only to worry about the teams.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there.
